paragraphs: On the sixth day of the third month, the court bell in Chang’an sounded half a watch earlier than usual.

Fu Jian had not slept all night. Before dawn, he ordered his attendants to spread out the empire’s great map, and set two other things beside it. One was the ledger of households still unsettled after the battle for Xiangyang. The other was news from south of the Huai: Xie Xuan had added shipyards along the river, and the Beifu Army, far from disbanding, had taken in another wave of refugees from the north. The messenger said that memorials had been submitted at Jiankang over the Xie family’s command of troops; the court was quarreling fiercely.

Fu Jian picked up the report and set it down again. He remembered the warning beside Wang Meng’s grave: “Be cautious in raising an army against the south.” A spring chill still lingered outside the palace. The ten-year pledge had not yet run its course. What had woken before its term was his own white hair.

At dawn the imperial guards opened the vermilion gates of Chongde Hall. Princes, Secretariat officials, finance officers, and commanders from the central army entered in order. Many still looked sleepy from the night before; one glance at the great map stretching from Hexi to the lands south of the Yangtze woke them all. The ministers unbuckled their swords and stood before the throne steps. Light mud marked the side of Fu Rong’s boots, picked up when he made his morning circuit past the granaries. The list of shipbuilding timber sent by Fu Pi from Nanyang was still tucked into his sleeve, its curled edge damp from his palm.

Zhu Xu did not stand among the ministers. He remained a Jin general residing as a guest under the Court for State Guests. Fu Jian had invited him to listen. The palace attendants laid a mat beside a screen on the east side: they would not demand that he call himself a subject of Qin, nor pretend he had wandered in by chance. He arrived dressed in the old Jin robes and cap. When an attendant removed his outer gown, Zhu Xu merely straightened its hem before sitting down.

Yao Chang had come too, his ceremonial robes as Minister of Ceremonies faultlessly arranged. His seat was in the rear rank, separated from the military commanders by an entire row. Since the mutiny at Wei Bridge, everyone in Chang’an knew that he observed the rites with exactness, while familiar faces still traveled quietly between his circle and the Qiang country. At the palace gate that morning, an old acquaintance selling incense bowed to him from afar. Yao Chang walked straight into the hall as though he had seen nothing.
Fu Jian stopped at the foot of the throne steps without mounting the throne.

“You know what we are here to discuss. Those who want war must tell me where the army will march once it has crossed the river, and how it will eat. Those who oppose it need not shelter themselves behind Wang Jinglüe’s honored name.”
No one dared to answer first. He turned the jade ring on his finger once, sat, and said, “Fu Pi, speak.”

Fu Pi knew the river charts by heart. Instead of beginning with a call to battle, he had an attendant lay a smaller chart over the great map. It showed the granaries, shipyards, and branching waterways from Xiangyang to the mouth of the Huai. He was far better prepared than he had been at the first discussions of Xiangyang.

“I visited the old camps on the Huai to investigate our defeat. The floating bridges were unsound. The river fleet was unequal to the task. By the time grain reached the crossings, nearly half was gone. The boats built at Xiangyang this year can remedy two of those failures. If we delay another year, the Beifu fleet will know every shallow branch of the river still better.”
He pressed his palm to the map, covering the ground where the army had been defeated.

“I ask that we begin with the two hundred and fifty thousand fit for an expedition, and raise a separate river fleet. If a better opportunity appears, we cannot simply watch it pass because two years remain on the pledge.”
At the last words, Fu Hong looked up. “Of the two hundred boats reported by the shipyards, how many have been into deep water?”
Fu Pi turned toward his younger brother. “One hundred and forty.”
“And how many of those can carry horses in heavy armor?”
“More than forty. The shipwrights are still altering their holds.”
“If we must ferry twenty thousand men across in one movement, how many trips?”

Fu Pi did not evade the question. “I have made the calculations. But the depths differ from one stretch of river to another, and one figure cannot serve for them all. When the boatmen come to the capital, I will bring them here to answer you.”

Fu Hong inclined his head and pressed him no further. Fu Pi wrote the dimensions of the new warships on the back of his court tablet. When he withdrew to his place, he no longer glared at the crown prince. A junior clerk of the Secretariat gathered Fu Hong’s registers of three districts short of grain; at the corner of a sheet one could see the date he had just added for inspecting the ships.

A military officer revived an argument from earlier councils: the new army needed one great war involving the whole state before Di, Xianbei, Qiang, and Han soldiers could truly fight with one heart. Fu Pi’s expression darkened. He had not forgotten the blood beneath Wei Bridge, nor why old comrades had turned their blades on one another in the same camp that night.

“If our armies can only hold together while they have an enemy,” he said, “must we find another enemy as soon as that war is won? I want victory. I do not want more men to die merely to prove the name of the state written on their rolls.”
He thought the words too blunt as soon as he had spoken them, and stepped back into line. His father did not praise him; he gave the ship chart only a quiet glance.

A Han official from the eastern commanderies, Cui Huai, requested leave to speak. His ancestors were buried in Hedong, while several cousins still lived south of the Yangtze. In letters, relatives in the north called those in the south “Jin slaves”; those in the south called him “a man lost to the north.” As he described his aging mother, now afraid even to ask whether her kin still lived, his voice suddenly roughened.

“If the realm remains divided forever, that does not mean an end to war. The Jiang-Huai region calls up men year after year. Refugees flee back and forth across the divide, while officials demand to know from which bank they came. I dare not say one war will make everything right. But I dare not say that never fighting again will make it right either.”

These were words bound up with his own grief. Some in the hall nodded faintly. Others whispered that because the Cui family yearned for reunion, must twenty-five ten-thousands of soldiers accompany him across the river? Cui Huai heard them. He tightened his grip on his court tablet and remained where he stood.
Yao Chang stepped out of the rear rank and bowed to Fu Jian. “I agree, Your Majesty, though my concern is not the fate of the Cui family alone.”
Fu Rong looked at him. “Minister Yao, have you put aside the rites for today?”

“The Minister of Ceremonies must also preside over sacrifices for those who die in war.” Yao Chang smiled, then let the smile fade. “I have seen Your Majesty pacify Guanzhong in your youth, then give a place to the Murong family, settle the Qiang, and win the allegiance of Hebei. If the historians of the future record only Qin’s northern borders, it would hardly do justice to the forces already assembled today.”
Fu Jian did not speak.

Yao Chang continued, “Xie An is aging too. But the Beifu Army is growing stronger. Affairs in the south may not wait until we have kept our promise for ten years. If a hundred years from now the realm is still divided in two, what will posterity say Your Majesty lacked?”

The question came softly, but Fu Jian heard the meaning hardest to acknowledge: someone could inherit your territory without inheriting the years you had been given to live. He had never cared much for splendid houses or beautiful women, nor was he consumed by feasting. Yet that stretch of country south of the river, untouched by Qin’s colors, had lain in his dreams for decades.
“Minister Yao,” Fu Rong said, “you speak of historians. Have you ever been to the barren banks of the Huai where the dead are buried?”

“The Duke of Yangping has. I have not.” Yao Chang did not quarrel. “But I have seen the sons of Qiang families who could never return home. One battle fewer does not always mean fewer dead; two more years of waiting may not be kinder than acting today.”
Fu Rong regarded him for a long time, but held back his anger. He knew Yao Chang could hide several paths in a single sentence. Block one, and another would remain open.
By the time Fu Rong’s turn came, the ceremonial attendants had replenished the lamp oil once.

He went to the map, placed one small wooden marker at Xiangyang, another north of the Huai, and a third at Jiankang. Many expected him to discuss the enemy army. Instead he picked up more markers and set them, one by one, at Jiangling, Xiakou, Guangling, and the ferry crossings upstream on the Yangtze.

“We besieged one city, Xiangyang, for months. When its walls fell, the Qin army could not simply hand every house to newly appointed officials and leave. You remember how many garrison men, grain officers, and workers repairing the levees had to stay.”
He moved half the markers away from the city.

“Suppose we take Jiankang. What of the land outside it? Jiangling? Guangling? If the Jin court retreats toward Kuaiji, do our fleets pursue? Every city we take must be held. Capture ten cities at the front, and we must detach men to ten places behind us. In a year, will we have gained ten cities or opened ten more mouths that must be fed?”
A commander replied, “Once the Jin main army is defeated, entire provinces will surrender of their own accord.”
Murong Chui turned his eyes back from the corridor outside. Fu Rong invited him to answer.
“Ye surrendered,” Murong Chui said. “Did every man of Yan cease drawing his sword after that?”
The commander instinctively glanced toward Murong Chui, whose old campaigns had been fought for Yan, and dared not reply.

Murong Chui bowed to Fu Jian. “I have won battles, and I have served as a general of a defeated country. You can take a city and replace its governor. What a lost kingdom leaves inside a man’s belly cannot be carved out in one night with a hundred thousand knives. Your Majesty gave me soldiers so that I might fight. You should not require me to promise that everyone will be glad when the fighting is over.”
Fu Jian asked, “If I defeat Xie Xuan on the Huai, will the south still resist?”
“Some will resist, and some will submit.”
“You cannot tell which?”
“Not until I am there.”

Fu Pi’s eyebrows moved. He had seen Murong Chui break through an enemy ring on horseback on a snowy plain and hold himself back from an assault at Xiangyang when the temptation was almost unbearable. He had not imagined such a commander would honestly answer his sovereign: *I do not know.*
“And if Yan rises while I am campaigning in the south?” Fu Jian suddenly asked.

Murong Chui was quiet for a moment. “The men I left behind in Yan are still alive. Some hate me for abandoning it. Others would come over if I said a single word. If all the northern troops are withdrawn, they will not necessarily guard Qin’s rear as obediently as you hope.”
A prince commanding troops instantly looked up. “General Who Champions the Army, are you warning the court to beware of you yourself?”
“I am.”

His answer was so frank that the prince had no reply. Fu Jian noticed the white at Murong Chui’s temples and remembered Wang Meng’s deathbed warning that a state could not rest upon one man’s lifelong loyalty. Now, spoken by the man most liable to suspicion, the words sounded more like the voice of the living than the inscription on a tomb.
When Fu Hong was called forward, he did not bring the whole mass of registers. He carried only a thin expedition book, with a yellow slip from the Secretariat pressed against its cover.

“Your son does not argue that we should never cross the Yangtze. An army of two hundred and fifty thousand, organized for distant service, can fight a great battle. But I ask Father first to have the military headquarters put in writing what this war is meant to take, and under what circumstances it will stop.”
“Destroy Jin,” Fu Jian said.
“If the Jin emperor leaves Jiankang for Kuaiji, will that count as its destruction?”
“Capture him.”
“And if the imperial clan enthrones another?”
Fu Jian did not answer.

Fu Hong pressed no further. He opened the old edict for Xiangyang instead. Before that limited expedition began, its orders had forbidden massacre, crossing beyond specified bounds, and staying past the appointed time. Some soldiers had broken those orders, but afterward it had still been possible to ask who had done so.

“If there is no place anywhere across a thousand *li* of southern country where the advance must end, then at every step our army can claim the war is unfinished. I fear that in the end the court will not even dare write down the day on which it should withdraw.”

Objections rose across the hall. Some said an army could hardly be sent out if its men were taught to think of retreat first. Others argued that plans changed constantly and deadlines would bind the commanders' hands. Fu Jian raised his hand and silenced them. He did not immediately rebuke Fu Hong. He knew his son had become far harder to deal with than before, and he would not send him away merely by invoking the authority of father and sovereign.
“Zhu Xu.” He beckoned toward the eastern side. “You defended Xiangyang for years. Tell us what the southerners will do if they see Qin soldiers cross the river.”
Zhu Xu stood and bowed according to the old rites of Jin. He had expected the question when they invited him, but not the eyes of everyone in the hall upon him.
“First they will close their gates.”
“I did not massacre Xiangyang.”

“After Xiangyang fell, I saw how Your Majesty restrained your soldiers,” Zhu Xu said. “But before the gates opened, the people inside could hear only the drums outside. They did not know what the Heavenly King would do.”
“Many scholars hate the harsh government of Jin,” Cui Huai observed.

“They do,” Zhu Xu said. “They hate the land taxes, and the way sons of great houses humiliate men from humbler families. There are fathers forced to surrender grain by Jin officials whose sons still defend Jin cities.”
“Why?” Fu Jian asked.

Zhu Xu glanced down at the faded embroidery on his sleeve. “My father once asked me, if our roof always leaked, would I let strangers tear the house down and rebuild it? I said yes. He asked what I would say if the strangers first came in with knives and killed the family members who refused to leave. Then I no longer knew how to answer.”

A military official snorted at this rustic example. Fu Jian did not laugh. He remembered a woman in Chang’an who had once sewn clothes for men of Jin, and an old man after Xiangyang who preferred his broken house to an immediate ration of Qin grain. An emperor could make promises to the world; the people of the world were under no obligation to believe him at once.
“If you were still within Jin’s borders,” Fu Jian asked, “would you defend it?”
“I would.”

Zhu Xu answered too quickly. For a moment no one in the hall knew whether anger was required. Fu Jian simply watched him, then ordered him escorted back to his guest quarters at the Court for State Guests. Zhu Xu left without bowing again as a subject to the Qin emperor.

The debate lasted the whole day. Some spoke of generations of suffering under the north-south division. Others warned that the treasury had only just recovered and must not repeat the disaster on the Huai. Some were eager for military distinction; others defended their provincial tax revenues. Private desires mixed with sound arguments. Fu Jian heard both plainly, yet was reluctant to dismiss any one speaker as a blind loyalist or a greedy seeker of glory.

As the sun sank, officials crowded the map in the hall, their sleeves pointing south until the paper darkened with wear. Fu Jian suddenly descended the throne steps and asked Fu Rong, “If we never raise an army, will Xie An make Jin stronger?”
“He will.”
“If we do, can I take Jiankang?”
“There is a chance.”
“How great a chance?”

Fu Rong hesitated. In all the years they had pacified revolts together and escorted grain convoys, his younger brother had always dared to find a way through danger for him. Yet now he would not give a perfect answer.
Fu Jian turned toward the lands south of the river, drawn in light ink, and smiled faintly.
“After a whole day of debate, not one man is willing to walk this road for me.”
Fu Rong said softly, “Your Majesty must walk it yourself in the end. All we can do is point out the pits along the way.”

Fu Jian was silent for a long time. Finally he said, “We will debate it again tomorrow. Do not rewrite tonight’s speeches into praises of my accomplishments. Record what each man said exactly as he said it.”

After court dispersed, a little evening glow remained outside the hall. Fu Pi put on his outer robe and reached the long steps. Fu Hong was still waiting beneath the corridor for the clerks to gather the scrolls. A bronze lamp stood between the brothers. Neither spoke for a long while.
“Those were good questions you asked today,” Fu Pi said at last.
Fu Hong turned.
“But do not imagine good questions will win the battle by themselves.”
Fu Hong looked at the corner of a naval chart protruding from his elder brother’s sleeve. “And do not imagine that because every boat is ready, no one will be waiting for you in the south.”
Fu Pi did not take offense. Instead he gave a short laugh. “I know. That is why I am still building them.”

He walked briskly into the night. Watching him go, Fu Hong began to understand what made the council so difficult: it was not that someone had spoken falsely, but that so many people who spoke with reason wanted different endings.

Inside Chengming Hall, Fu Jian had not yet ordered the map removed. The lightly shaded patch of southern country glimmered white in the lamplight. He stood alone before it for a long time. Then he told the attendant to fetch a fresh blank sheet of imperial edict paper.
“What is Your Majesty drafting tonight?”
“Luoyang.”
“A royal progress, or the movement of troops?”
Fu Jian looked at the paper without answering at once.
Outside, a night watch drum sounded. Far across Chang’an, some had already fallen asleep to the beat.
